captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 3: Cells.
Have you ever wondered what you are really made of?
Today we will discover what cells are, what is inside them,
how they do special jobs,
and how they work together to build a living thing.
How big is a cell?
Let's compare some real things, from big to very small.
The point of a pin is about one and a half millimetres across.
You can easily see it.
A grain of salt is about 0.3 millimetres.
It is tiny, but you can still see it.
A human hair is about 0.1 millimetres wide.
This is close to the smallest thing your eyes can see.
One of your cheek cells is about 0.06 millimetres across.
That is too small to see without a microscope.
A red blood cell is even smaller: about 0.008 millimetres.
And a bacterium can be just 0.002 millimetres long.
Most cells are between 0.01 and 0.1 millimetres.
Predict: how many cheek cells, side by side,
would be as wide as one grain of salt?
Pause and work it out.
Every living thing – from the smallest bacterium to the largest whale –
is built from cells.
Think of a brick wall.
Each brick is a small part that builds the whole wall.
In the same way,
your body is built from millions of tiny building blocks called cells.
All living things – called organisms – are made up of cells.
Plants and animals are made of many cells.
They are multicellular organisms.
We are multicellular too.
Some organisms are only one single cell.
They are unicellular organisms, such as bacteria and yeast.
Organisms so small that we need a microscope to see them are called microorganisms.
All unicellular organisms are microorganisms.
Unicellular organisms are all around us.
Here are three everyday examples.
When bread dough rises, millions of yeast cells are at work.
Each yeast cell is a whole organism.
Yoghurt is made by bacteria.
They change milk into yoghurt, and each bacterium is just one cell.
A single drop of pond water can contain an Amoeba.
It moves, feeds and grows, all inside one cell.
How did scientists find out about cells?
Our ideas developed step by step over many years.
Around 1021, the Muslim scholar Ibn al-Haytham explained how lenses work.
Microscopes depend on lenses.
Robert Hooke looked at cork through a compound microscope.
He saw tiny boxes that looked like small rooms, and called them cells.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made very good lenses that magnified about 200 times.
He was able to see unicellular organisms.
In 1839, Schleiden (who studied plants) and Schwann (who
studied animals) shared their findings and developed cell theory.
About 15 years later, Rudolf Virchow added a new idea:
all cells come from cells that already exist.
Cell theory has three main statements.
One: all living things are made up of one or more cells.
Two: cells are the basic units of life.
Three, added by Virchow: all cells come from pre-existing cells –
cells that were already there.
This shows that scientific theories can change and grow when new discoveries are made.
We use a light microscope to see cells.
Let's learn its main parts.
The eyepiece is the lens we look through.
The objective lens is close to the specimen and magnifies it.
The specimen slide sits on the stage.
Stage clips hold the slide still.
We turn the coarse and fine adjustment wheels to get a sharp,
clear image.
The light source shines light through the specimen,
and the diaphragm controls how much light reaches it.
We carry the microscope by holding the arm and the base.
The base keeps it stable.
It is called a light microscope because light
passes through the object we are looking at.
To look at cells, we first prepare a specimen slide.
Place a thin piece of the specimen –
the object we want to observe – on a glass slide.
Add a tiny drop of liquid, such as water.
Carefully lower a thin coverslip over the specimen.
Then place the slide on the microscope stage.
Stay safe: never point a microscope mirror at the Sun,
and handle coverslips carefully.
A student looks down a microscope at an onion slide,
but sees only a dark, blurry circle.
Predict: which part should she change first?
Pause and choose.
Watch. She opens the diaphragm.
More light passes through the specimen, and the view becomes bright.
The view is bright now, but blurry.
With the lowest-power lens, she slowly turns the coarse focusing knob.
The onion cells come into focus!
To see more detail she can change to a higher-power lens,
and then use only the fine knob.
Explain what happened: the diaphragm controls how much light reaches the specimen,
and focusing makes the image sharp.
If you still see nothing,
check that the slide is over the hole in the stage.
Now let's use the microscope correctly.
Always start with the lowest-power objective lens.
Bring the image into focus using the coarse adjustment wheel.
When you change to a higher-power lens, use only the fine adjustment wheel.
The coarse wheel could push the lens into the slide and damage it.
Remember: cells look flat under the microscope, but they are really three-dimensional.
Total magnification = magnification of the eyepiece lens × magnification of the objective lens.
Example: an eyepiece of ×10 and an objective lens
of ×15 give a total magnification of ×150.
Try this: van Leeuwenhoek's lens magnified ×200.
How long would a 0.1 mm object appear?
Pause and work it out.
The object would look 20 millimetres long.

captions: This diagram is a model of a typical plant cell.
Let's look at each part.
The nucleus controls all the cell's activities.
It contains strands of DNA.
The cytoplasm is a jelly-like material.
Materials are made and broken down in it.
The cell membrane is a thin layer around the cell.
It controls what goes in and out.
Mitochondria release energy from food by chemical reactions called aerobic respiration.
The cell wall is strong and stiff, made of cellulose.
It supports the cell and gives it a regular shape.
Chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll,
which captures light energy so the plant can make food by photosynthesis.
The large sap vacuole is filled with cell sap.
It takes in water to keep the cell firm.
You can see these parts yourself by looking at onion cells under a microscope.
Why is a fresh lettuce leaf crisp, but an old one floppy?
The answer is inside its cells.
In a fresh leaf, each sap vacuole is full of water.
It pushes outwards against the strong cell wall, so the cell is firm.
When the leaf loses water, the vacuoles shrink.
The cells are no longer pushed firm, so the leaf goes floppy.
Try it at home: put a floppy leaf in cold water.
The vacuoles fill up again and the leaf becomes crisp.
Now an animal cell,
for example a cell from the inside of your cheek.
Like a plant cell,
it has a nucleus that controls the cell and contains DNA.
The cytoplasm fills most of the animal cell.
A thin cell membrane surrounds the cell and controls what goes in and out.
Mitochondria release energy from food by aerobic respiration.
You can observe cheek cells safely using a sterile cotton bud –
only use cells from your own body.
Cheek cells are almost colourless, so they are very hard to see.
Predict: what will happen when we add one
drop of a blue stain called methylene blue?
Pause and choose.
Watch carefully as the drop lands on the cells and spreads under the coverslip.
Now the cells are pale blue, and each nucleus is dark blue.
The cell membrane shows the edge of each cell.
Explain what you saw: the stain colours the parts of the cell,
especially the nucleus, so the cells stand out from the clear background.
For onion cells, scientists often use iodine solution instead.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Predict: if you look at the thin layer from inside an onion bulb,
will you see green chloroplasts?
Pause and decide.
Here is a leaf cell next to an onion bulb cell.
The leaf cell is packed with chloroplasts.
The onion cell has none.
The onion bulb grows underground, where there is no light.
Its cells cannot photosynthesise, so they do not need chloroplasts.
Remember: every plant cell has a cell wall,
but not every plant cell has chloroplasts.
Let's compare plant cells and animal cells.
Both have a nucleus, cytoplasm, a cell membrane and mitochondria.
Only plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large sap vacuole.
In an animal cell, the cytoplasm fills almost the whole cell.
In a plant cell,
the large sap vacuole takes up most of the space.
Animal cells usually have more mitochondria,
because animals move much more and need more energy.
Think about it: why do plant cells need cell walls,
but animal cells do not?
Hint: think of tall trees.
Scientists use models to explain things that are hard to see.
Here is a model plant cell made from everyday objects.
The box is the cell wall, food wrap is the cell membrane,
a bag of water is the sap vacuole,
a grape is the nucleus and green peas are chloroplasts.
A strength of this model: it shows the parts and where they are,
and it is three-dimensional, like a real cell.
A limitation: it is far too big,
the food wrap cannot control what goes in and out,
and there are no mitochondria or cytoplasm.
Every model has strengths and limitations.

captions: A multicellular organism has different types of cells.
Their shapes and structures let them do specific jobs.
We say they are specialised.
A root hair cell has a long extension that pushes out into the soil.
This extension increases the surface area of the cell,
so it can absorb water and mineral salts quickly.
A palisade cell is found near the upper surface of a leaf.
It is tall and column-shaped, with many chloroplasts.
This lets it absorb a lot of light energy for photosynthesis.
Water moves from the soil into a root hair cell,
and then into its sap vacuole.
Predict: in which order does it pass through the parts of the cell?
Pause and put them in order.
First, water passes through the cell wall.
The wall is strong but lets water through.
Next it crosses the cell membrane, which controls what goes in and out.
Then it moves through the cytoplasm…
…and finally into the sap vacuole.
So the order is: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, sap vacuole.
Because the root hair is long and thin,
it has a large surface touching the soil water,
so lots of water can enter quickly.
Animals have specialised cells too.
Ciliated cells line our air passages.
Their cilia beat together to move mucus and trapped dust away from the lungs.
Red blood cells contain haemoglobin to carry oxygen.
They have no nucleus,
and their dimpled disc shape gives a large surface area to take up oxygen quickly.
Nerve cells, or neurones, carry electrical impulses.
Branched endings receive messages and a long fibre carries them quickly.
Amazing fact: some nerve cells are as thin as
a hair but up to a metre long!
When cells share out different jobs, we call it division of labour.
In a healthy airway, the cilia beat together.
They sweep sticky mucus, with trapped dust and bacteria, up to the throat,
where it is swallowed.
Chemicals in cigarette smoke stop the cilia from beating.
Predict: what will happen to the mucus?
Pause and choose.
Watch: the cilia are still, so the mucus is not swept away.
It builds up in the airways.
Dust and bacteria stay in the airways.
That is why smokers often have a cough, and get more chest infections.
Pause and explain this using the words cilia and mucus.
Some athletes train high in the mountains.
Why?
High up, the air is thinner.
Each breath brings in fewer oxygen particles.
After a few weeks, the body makes more red blood cells.
More red blood cells means more haemoglobin,
so more oxygen can be carried to the muscles.
This is a real example of structure linked to function.

captions: Next, how are cells organised in a multicellular organism?
A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to perform a function.
Plant tissues include epidermal tissue, which protects the plant, xylem, which carries water,
and phloem, which carries food.
Animal tissues include muscle, nerve, fat, epithelial and bone tissue.
Each one has its own job.
Let's cut a leaf open and look at its tissues.
Predict: why is the palisade layer found just below the top surface of the leaf?
Pause and choose.
The top layer is the upper epidermis.
Its cells are thin and clear, so light passes straight through.
Just below is the palisade layer.
Its tall cells are packed with chloroplasts,
so they absorb most of the light.
Being near the top means they get the most light.
Next comes the spongy layer.
It has air spaces,
so gases such as carbon dioxide can move around the leaf.
At the bottom is the lower epidermis,
with tiny pores that let gases in and out.
A leaf is an organ.
Each layer is a tissue, and the tissues work together to make food.
Watch out: some science words have an everyday meaning too.
In everyday life, a tissue is a soft paper handkerchief.
In science, a tissue is a group of similar cells working together,
like the ciliated epithelium that lines your airways.
Different tissues group together to form organs.
An organ is made of different tissues that work together.
Organs carry out important functions.
Plant organs: flowers help the plant reproduce,
the stem supports it and moves water, leaves make food,
and roots absorb water and anchor the plant.
Human organs include the brain, eyes, lungs, heart and stomach.
Each has its own function.
Organs work together in organ systems.
Several organs working together form an organ system.
Each system has a different job.
In plants, the roots, stem and leaves form the water transport system.
The root system anchors the plant,
and flowers are part of the reproductive system.
Humans have 11 organ systems.
Here are six: skeletal, respiratory, muscular, circulatory, digestive and excretory.
Let's put it all together.
It starts with a cell, for example a muscle cell.
Similar cells form a tissue – muscle tissue.
Different tissues form an organ, such as the heart.
Organs work together in an organ system –
the heart and blood vessels form the circulatory system.
All the organ systems together make the whole organism – a human being.
Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.
Every level works together so the organism functions efficiently.
Isn't it amazing that it all starts with a tiny cell?
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Which type of organism has only one cell?
Give an example. Pause the video now.
Answer: Unicellular – e.g.
bacterium, yeast, Amoeba.
Question 2: Name three parts found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
Pause the video now.
Answer: Cell wall, chloroplasts, large sap vacuole.
Question 3: An eyepiece is ×10 and the objective lens is ×40.
What is the total magnification?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 10 × 40 = 400, so the total magnification is ×400.
Question 4: Why does a root hair cell have a long extension?
Pause the video now.
Answer: A larger surface area, so it absorbs water and mineral salts quickly.
